answers: Greet the guest, then confirm the reservation, then ask for the passport, then hand over the key. Following this order keeps everything smooth.

feedback.text: Greet the guest, then confirm the reservation, then ask for the passport, then hand over the key. Following this order keeps everything smooth.

prompts.stem: 3. Put the check-in steps in the right order: hand over the key, greet the guest, ask for the passport, confirm the reservation.

answers: Something like “Could I see your passport, please?” A single word can feel like an order, so add “Could I,” the person’s help, and “please.”

feedback.text: Something like “Could I see your passport, please?” A single word can feel like an order, so add “Could I,” the person’s help, and “please.”

prompts.stem: 4. Make this sound polite: a colleague says “Passport.” How would you soften it?

feedback.text: B. “Could I ... please?” is the polite, service-friendly form.

prompts.stem: Q1. Which is the most polite way to ask for a document? A) “Give me your ID.” B) “Could I see your ID, please?” C) “ID.”

feedback.text: A. A guest with no reservation is a walk-in guest.

prompts.stem: Q2. A guest arrives with no booking. They are a ... A) walk-in guest B) key card C) voucher

feedback.text: A. “Is that correct?” confirms the details clearly and politely.

prompts.stem: Q3. Which phrase best confirms the booking details? A) “Is that correct?” B) “Who cares?” C) “Maybe.”

feedback.text: B. “Enjoy your stay” leaves a warm final impression.

prompts.stem: Q4. What is a warm way to close the interaction? A) “Bye.” B) “Enjoy your stay.” C) “Next.”

feedback.text: B. The key and the practical details, such as floor, breakfast, and Wi-Fi, naturally go together near the end.

prompts.stem: Q5. When do you usually share breakfast and Wi-Fi information? A) before greeting B) when you hand over the key C) never

feedback.text: B. Warmth, empathy, and efficient action together make strong hospitality.

prompts.stem: Q6. A guest looks exhausted. Which reply shows the best hospitality? A) “Sign here.” B) “Welcome. You must have had a long trip, so let us get you checked in quickly so you can rest.” C) “Hurry up, please.”

feedback.text: B. Amenities are the extras, such as Wi-Fi, a gym, or a pool.

prompts.stem: Q7. “Amenities” means ... A) complaints B) the extra services and facilities C) room numbers

feedback.text: B. Offering to hold their luggage keeps the guest comfortable and shows you care.

prompts.stem: Q8. The room is not ready yet. What is the best thing to do? A) tell the guest to come back later B) offer to store their luggage while they wait C) ignore the problem

feedback.text: “Good evening, welcome to the Grand Serenata Hotel. Yes, we do have a room available for tonight, a lovely Deluxe Room. Would you like to take it? Wonderful. I will just need your passport and a card for the deposit, and I will have you checked in right away.” This works because it greets warmly, offers a clear solution, and moves smoothly into the steps.

prompts.stem: Prompt: A walk-in guest with no reservation asks, “Do you have any rooms available for tonight?” Greet them, respond, and guide them into starting a check-in.

feedback.text: (a) “I do not know. Check your email.” This is unhelpful and pushes the problem back to the guest.
(b) “No problem at all, let me check that for you. May I have your name, please?” This is the ideal answer. It reassures the guest and moves calmly to the next step.
(c) “That is not my job.” This is rude and unprofessional.

prompts.stem: Guest: “Hi, I think I have a booking, but I am not sure it went through.”

feedback.text: (a) “Let me see what I can do for you. We have a room on the fourth floor with a city view. Would that suit you?” This is the ideal answer, because it offers a solution warmly.
(b) “Maybe. We will see.” This is vague and sounds dismissive.
(c) “All rooms are the same.” This shuts the guest down instead of helping.

prompts.stem: Guest: “Can I have a room on a high floor with a nice view?”

feedback.text: (a) “No, check-in is at 2. Come back later.” This is cold and unhelpful.

(b) “Let me check whether your room is ready. If it is not quite ready yet, I would be happy to store your luggage so you can relax in the meantime.” This is the ideal answer, warm and solution-focused.
(c) “That is against the rules.” This hides behind policy instead of helping.

prompts.stem: Guest: “I know I am very early, but is it possible to check in now?”

prompts.stem: Q1. What is the best way to answer a hotel phone? A) “Yeah?” B) “Good morning, the Grand Serenata Hotel, Maya speaking. How may I help you?” C) “Who is this?”

feedback.text: B. It pauses the call while you check something.

prompts.stem: Q2. “To put someone on hold” means ... A) to end the call B) to pause the call politely C) to transfer the call

feedback.text: B. Reading back is your safety net against errors.

prompts.stem: Q3. Why should you read a guest’s details back? A) to fill time B) to catch mistakes before they become booking errors C) it is polite but pointless

feedback.text: B. It gives the reference and ends on a welcoming note.

prompts.stem: Q4. What is a warm way to close? A) “Bye.” B) “Your booking reference is 452. Thank you for calling, and we look forward to welcoming you.” C) “That is all.”

feedback.text: B. Stay patient and help them hear you.

prompts.stem: Q5. The line is unclear. What should you do? A) hang up B) politely ask them to repeat, or repeat slowly yourself C) shout

feedback.text: A. You repeat the details out loud to confirm them.

prompts.stem: Q6. “To read back” the details means ... A) to confirm them by repeating them B) to read a book C) to cancel the booking

feedback.text: B. Single digits are the clearest on a call.

prompts.stem: Q7. How should you say the reference 452 on the phone? A) “four hundred fifty-two” quickly B) “four, five, two” as single digits C) spell it as letters

feedback.text: B. Explain, then transfer, so the caller always feels looked after.

prompts.stem: Q8. A caller needs the restaurant, not reservations. What is best? A) say “wrong number” B) transfer them warmly and tell them what you are doing C) hang up

feedback.text: “Good afternoon, the Grand Serenata Hotel, Maya speaking. How may I help you? ... I would be happy to help. Let me check availability for those two nights. ... Yes, we have a room. prompts.stem: Prompt: A caller wants to book two nights next week. Answer the phone, take the booking, confirm the details, and close the call.

feedback.text: (a) “I do not know.” Unhelpful, and it leaves the caller stuck.

(c) “Probably not.” Vague and discouraging.

prompts.stem: Caller: “Do you have any rooms for this Saturday?”

feedback.text: (a) “I already said it.” Rude, and it makes the caller feel bad.
(b) “Of course. Your booking reference is four, five, two. Shall I say it again slowly?” This is the ideal answer, patient and clear.
(c) Hanging up. Never do this.

prompts.stem: Caller: “Sorry, the line is a little unclear. Could you repeat that?”

feedback.text: (a) “Wrong number.” Cold and unhelpful.
(b) “Of course, I will put you through to our restaurant now. One moment, please.” This is the ideal answer, because it transfers the caller warmly and clearly.

feedback.text: A. The guest’s needs come first, even when you are busy.

prompts.stem: Q4. “Customer-centered” means ... A) focused on the guest’s needs B) focused only on speed C) focused only on the rules

feedback.text: (b). “Kind regards,” is warm and professional. The others are far too casual for a guest.

prompts.stem: 2. Choose the right sign-off for a formal reply: (a) “xoxo” or (b) “Kind regards,” or (c) “later!”

feedback.text: B. “Dear” with a title and surname is the formal standard.

prompts.stem: Q1. What is the best formal greeting? A) “Yo,” B) “Dear Mr. Chen,” C) “Hey there,”

feedback.text: A. It is warm and professional.

prompts.stem: Q2. What is the best formal sign-off? A) “Kind regards,” B) “cya,” C) “thx,”

feedback.text: A. It gently invites any further questions.

prompts.stem: Q3. “Please do not hesitate to contact us” is used to ... A) end warmly and offer more help B) refuse the guest C) rush the guest

feedback.text: A. A professional register represents the hotel well.

prompts.stem: Q4. With a guest, you should generally use a ... A) formal and warm register B) very casual register C) no greeting at all

feedback.text: B. Greeting first, sign-off last.

prompts.stem: Q5. What is the correct order of an email? A) sign-off, then body, then greeting B) greeting, then opening, then body, then sign-off C) body, then greeting, then sign-off

feedback.text: A. Apologise, take ownership, and offer a clear fix.

prompts.stem: Q6. When replying to a complaint email, the tone should be ... A) apologetic and solution-focused B) defensive C) silent

feedback.text: B. A clear subject line sets the topic before the guest even opens the message.

prompts.stem: Q7. Why does a clear subject line matter? A) it does not B) it helps the guest understand and find the email C) it replaces the greeting

feedback.text: B. Short lines and small lists are easy to scan on a phone.

prompts.stem: Q8. Which body is easiest for a guest to read quickly? A) one long paragraph B) short lines or a small bulleted list C) no spacing at all

feedback.text: “Dear Ms. Putri, thank you for your booking. We are pleased to confirm a Deluxe Room for one night, arriving next Friday, at 80 dollars per night, breakfast included. Your booking reference is four, six, one. We look forward to welcoming you. Kind regards, Maya, Grand Serenata Hotel.”

prompts.stem: Prompt: Write a short booking-confirmation email for a guest who reserved one night in a Deluxe Room, arriving next Friday.

feedback.text: (a) “Yes.” Too short, and it answers only half of the question.

(b) “Dear Guest, thank you for your enquiry. Yes, we have a Double Room available this weekend at 90 dollars per night, breakfast included. Please let us know if you would like to book. Kind regards, Maya.” This is the ideal answer, complete, tidy, and warm.
(c) “idk, check the website.” Unhelpful and far too casual.

prompts.stem: A guest writes: “Do you have a room for two people this weekend, and is breakfast included?”

feedback.text: (a) No reply at all. Silence makes the situation worse.

(b) “Dear Mr. Chen, thank you for letting us know, and please accept our sincere apologies. We have reviewed your bill and are correcting the duplicate charge now. The refund should appear within three to five days. Kind regards, Maya.” This is the ideal answer, an apology, ownership, and a clear action.
(c) “That is not our fault.” Defensive and cold, and it will only anger the guest further.

prompts.stem: A guest writes an upset email about being charged twice.

feedback.text: (a) “No.” Blunt and unfriendly.

(b) “Dear Ms. Putri, thank you for your message. We would be happy to offer a late check-out until 2 in the afternoon at no extra charge. Please let us know if that suits you. Kind regards, Maya.” This is the ideal answer, warm, clear, and helpful.
(c) “That depends.” Vague, and it leaves the guest unsure.

prompts.stem: A guest writes to ask for a late check-out.

prompts.stem: Q1. What is the first step when a guest complains? A) defend the hotel B) listen C) offer a discount straight away

feedback.text: B. It is sincere and specific.

prompts.stem: Q2. Which is a sincere apology? A) “Rules are rules.” B) “I sincerely apologise for the inconvenience.” C) “Calm down.”

feedback.text: B. You own the fix, personally.

prompts.stem: Q3. “Taking ownership” means ... A) blaming the system B) accepting responsibility and acting C) sending the guest away

feedback.text: A. For example, a free breakfast or an upgrade.

prompts.stem: Q4. A “goodwill gesture” is ... A) a kind extra to make up for the problem B) a punishment C) an official complaint form

feedback.text: B. Never deflect, blame, or dismiss.

prompts.stem: Q5. What are the three things to never do? A) listen, apologise, act B) deflect, blame, dismiss C) refund, upgrade, follow up

feedback.text: A. Following up is what shows the guest you truly care.

prompts.stem: Q6. What is the purpose of the follow-up step? A) to reassure the guest and confirm it is resolved B) to end the conversation quickly C) to charge the guest again

feedback.text: B. You can be sorry for the experience without assigning blame.

prompts.stem: Q7. A guest is angry and it is not your fault. What should you apologise for? A) nothing, since it is not your fault B) their poor experience, because it is about their feelings C) only if a manager tells you to

feedback.text: A. It is the art of winning a guest back after something went wrong.

prompts.stem: Q8. What is “service recovery”? A) turning an unhappy guest back into a happy one B) repairing broken equipment C) recovering a lost booking

feedback.text: “I am very sorry to hear that, and I understand how frustrating it is to lose the Wi-Fi all day. This is the Listen and Apologise part. Let me send our technician to your room right away, and I will switch you to our backup network in the meantime. This is the Act part. As an apology, I would like to offer you a late check-out, and I will check back within the hour to make sure it is working. This is the Follow up part.”

prompts.stem: Prompt: A guest complains that the Wi-Fi has not worked all day. Handle it using the L-A-A-F framework.

feedback.text: (a) “Housekeeping usually does a good job.” This deflects instead of helping.

(b) “I am so sorry, that is not our standard at all. I will have it cleaned immediately, or I can move you to another room right now. Which would you prefer?” This is the ideal answer, an apology, ownership, and a choice of solution.
(c) “Are you sure it is dirty?” This dismisses the guest and will only make it worse.

prompts.stem: Guest: “My room is dirty. This is unacceptable.”

feedback.text: (a) “That is the system’s fault, not mine.” This blames something else and helps no one.
(b) “I am very sorry for the error. Let me check your bill and correct it right away, and you will see the refund shortly.” This is the ideal answer, an apology, action, and reassurance.
(c) “You must have made a mistake.” This blames the guest, which is the fastest way to lose them.

prompts.stem: Guest: “You charged me twice.”

feedback.text: (a) “Well, nobody is perfect.” Dismissive and cold.

(b) “I am truly sorry, and I understand why you are frustrated after a second issue. Let me put this right now, and I will speak with my manager to make sure it does not happen again.” This is the ideal answer, empathy, action, and a follow-up promise.
(c) “There is nothing I can do.” This gives up on the guest entirely.

prompts.stem: Guest: “This is the second time I have had a problem here.”

outcomes.statement: Can identify warmth, attentiveness and problem-solving in a hotel customer-care situation.
Can replace a negative service response with a simple, positive next-step response.
Can record confidence and choose a next practice action without treating self-rating as proficiency.
Can greet a guest, confirm a reservation and close a routine check-in warmly.
Can request identification and confirm room and stay details accurately.
Can explain key-card, breakfast and hotel information and offer further help.
Can open and close a routine hotel telephone call professionally.
Can clarify, spell and read back caller details to confirm accuracy.
Can take a short message and place, hold or transfer a call politely.
Can identify a hotline caller’s room and service need.
Can take and read back a routine order and communicate an estimated time.
Can transfer a request to the correct department and state a follow-up action.
Can structure a clear service email with suitable opening, body, action and close.
Can confirm booking or enquiry details accurately in writing.
Can respond to a written concern with thanks, apology, action and further-help language.
Can produce a brief, warm and professional reply in live chat or social media.
Can handle a routine online request using formulaic service language and clarification.
Can move a sensitive public complaint to a private channel and escalate with a clear next step.
Can listen, acknowledge impact and apologise without blaming or dismissing the guest.
Can explain the problem, take ownership and offer an appropriate solution or next action.
Can follow up a complaint orally or in writing to confirm resolution.
